guide.title: Who Has Seen the Wind? — a guided memorization plan
guide.description: A gentle two-day guided plan to read, enjoy, and memorize Christina Rossetti’s “Who Has Seen the Wind?”, one stanza at a time, with a friendly return to yesterday’s lines.

metadata.voice: warm, poetry-loving friend with scholar’s depth
metadata.chunkingStrategy: one stanza per session, split into chunks of at most two lines

poem.title: Who Has Seen the Wind?
poem.author: Christina Rossetti
poem.text:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling
The wind is passing thro’.

Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.

metadata.form: two quatrains, ABCB rhyme in each stanza
metadata.textEdition: Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book, Macmillan, 1893; retains the printed contraction thro’.

coverImage.alt: Oil painting of a leafy tree bending in a breeze beside an open green meadow under a cloudy sky.

lines.text: But when the leaves hang trembling

sessions.title: A Little Mystery in the Leaves
sessions.subtitle: Day 1 of 2
sessions.focusSummary: Meet the whole poem, then learn the first stanza by following its question, answer, and trembling leaves.

pages.title: The Whole Poem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling
The wind is passing thro’.

Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.

pages.title: Today's Lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Today we’ll keep company with the first four lines. Read them slowly once or twice. The little word “thro’” means “through” and sounds exactly the same.

pages.title: Come and Look with Me
pages.bodyMarkdown:
I love how Rossetti makes room for us straight away: “Neither I nor you.” We’re standing beside the speaker, looking at the same leaves. Nobody can see the wind itself, but we can see what it touches.

Notice the turn at “But.” The question opens a mystery; the trembling leaves offer a way to understand it. Try holding that small scene in your mind as you learn the words. A branch outside a window will do beautifully.

pages.title: Meet Christina Rossetti
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was born in London into a family of writers and artists. Her brother Dante Gabriel was a painter and poet, and Christina began writing poetry while she was young.

She wrote the rich, strange *Goblin Market*, devotional poems, and verses for children. Here she gives a very ordinary moment her full attention. It’s a lovely invitation to slow down and look with her.

pages.title: Last-Word 1/2
pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the rhyme lend a hand. Restore the last word of each line, then say the line aloud. Take your time.

pages.title: Last-Word 2/2
pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the rhyme lend a hand. Restore the last word of each line, then say the line aloud. Take your time.

pages.title: Let the Rhymes Bring You Home
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Say “you” and “thro’” aloud: they rhyme, giving the second and fourth lines a soft landing. The question sounds conversational, while “But when the leaves hang trembling” seems to linger on its branch.

You can let the rhythm help without marching through it. For a memory path, try **question → you → leaves → through**. Then put the little connecting words back. The scene and the sound can carry the lines together.

pages.title: A Small Poem with Room to Wonder
pages.bodyMarkdown:
This poem belongs to *Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book*, first published in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes. Its short verses make room for animals, weather, play, and questions.

We’re keeping the spelling “thro’” from the 1893 edition used here. It’s simply a shortened way of writing “through.” Read it naturally, as if you were talking with someone beside you.

pages.title: A Moment to Reflect
pages.prompt: When did you last notice the wind through something it moved: leaves, a curtain, someone’s hair? Which image would you like to keep beside these lines?

pages.title: A Stanza to Take Outside
pages.bodyMarkdown:
You’ve spent a little time with four lovely lines. Before you go, try saying them once while picturing those leaves. If a word wanders off, have a look and welcome it back.

Tomorrow we’ll return to this stanza, then let our gaze travel from the leaves to the whole tree. Next time a branch stirs, you may find the opening question waiting for you.

sessions.title: When the Trees Bow
sessions.subtitle: Day 2 of 2
sessions.focusSummary: Recall the first stanza, learn the second, and connect the two through their small, memorable changes.

pages.title: A Look Back
pages.bodyMarkdown: Welcome back. Before we read again, let’s visit yesterday’s lines. Try what you remember, then take a peek if you need one. Every return helps the words feel more familiar.

pages.title: Yesterday's Lines 1/2
pages.bodyMarkdown: Find the first and last word of each line from yesterday, then try saying the whole line. A quick look is always welcome.

pages.title: The Whole Poem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling
The wind is passing thro’.

Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.

pages.title: Today's Lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the second stanza gently. Picture the whole tree bending this time. Let “Neither you nor I” and “passing by” settle together in your ear.

pages.title: From a Leaf to a Whole Tree
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Yesterday we watched the leaves tremble. Now the trees “bow down their heads.” That human gesture is called *personification*: Rossetti lets us recognize a familiar movement in a tree. You might hear a courteous bow, or feel the weight of a stronger breeze.

I like the way our view widens without leaving the little scene. First a leaf, then a whole tree: the wind remains invisible, and its presence becomes easier to feel.

pages.title: An Ear for Little Changes
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Rossetti’s care with small words is easy to hear here. Read “Neither I nor you,” then “Neither you nor I.” The people haven’t changed; their order has. That tiny exchange makes a new rhyme possible.

Try the two phrases aloud as if you were offering someone a turn in a conversation. Her craft feels wonderfully companionable: the poem keeps bringing the reader back into the circle.

pages.title: Last-Word 1/2

pages.title: Last-Word 2/2

pages.title: Two Pairs to Keep Beside You
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Here’s a friendly way through the nearly matching stanzas: **you / thro’** belongs with the leaves; **I / by** belongs with the trees. The rhyme helps you choose the right order of the pronouns.

Both stanzas begin “Who has seen the wind?” and turn at “But when.” Keep those shared stepping stones, then let each picture supply its own words. Try whispering the rhyme pairs before your next round.

pages.title: First-Letter 2/2

pages.title: The Question We Get to Keep
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The poem answers its question by asking us to look carefully. The speaker and reader cannot see the wind, but they can notice its passing. That leaves room for wonder as well as understanding.

You may find other meanings gathering around that thought. Let them come in their own time. For now, these two small scenes are plenty: trembling leaves, bowing trees, and us there to notice.

pages.title: A Moment to Reflect
pages.prompt: How does the feeling change for you when the leaves become trees that “bow down their heads”? What sort of voice would you use for the repeated question?

pages.title: Eight Lines for a Breezy Day
pages.bodyMarkdown:
You’ve visited all eight lines. When you feel ready, try the whole poem aloud with the words covered: question, leaves; question, trees. If the pronouns swap places, let “you / thro’” and “I / by” guide you home.

Come back tomorrow for a quiet read and another try from memory, then again a few days later. I hope these lines keep you company outdoors. There’s something lovely about having a poem ready when the world gives you its opening image.
